title: Build an LRU cache with TTLs
prompt:
Build the in-memory cache that sits in front of the reading app's getBook(bookId) call. It holds at most capacity entries. When it is full and a new key arrives, it evicts the least recently used key (the one nobody has read or written for the longest). Entries can also carry a time to live (TTL), measured with an injected clock so the tests are deterministic.

API:

  • new LRUCache(capacity, now): now is a function returning the current time in ms (defaults to () => 0).
  • set(key, value, ttlMs): store or overwrite. ttlMs is optional; without it the entry never expires. Overwriting resets the TTL and counts as a use.
  • get(key): returns the value, or undefined if missing or expired. A hit counts as a use. An entry set at time t with ttlMs = 100 is expired once now() >= t + 100; delete it when you notice.
  • size(): number of entries currently stored.

Example: capacity 2. set('a',1); set('b',2); get('a'); set('c',3) evicts b, because a was used more recently.

Tip: a JavaScript Map remembers insertion order, and map.keys().next().value is the oldest key.

tests.name: stores and reads values; missing keys are undefined
evicts the least recently used key when full
a get counts as a use
overwriting a key updates it without evicting anything
entries expire exactly at set time + ttl (injected clock)
entries without a ttl never expire
overwriting resets the ttl
capacity 1 always keeps only the latest key

hints: Use the Map's insertion order as your recency list: the first key is the least recently used, the last key is the most recently used.
To mark a key as "just used", delete it and set it again. That moves it to the end. Do this on every hit and every overwrite.

Store { value, expiresAt } where expiresAt = ttlMs === undefined ? Infinity : now() + ttlMs. In get, if now() >= expiresAt, delete and return undefined. In set, only evict this.map.keys().next().value when the key is new and the map is full.
explain:
You just built the core of what Redis does with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru plus EXPIRE, and what every CDN edge does with its disk. Real systems approximate LRU (Redis samples a handful of keys instead of keeping a perfect list) because a perfect list costs memory per key, and they expire keys both lazily (on read, like you did) and with a background sweep so dead keys do not sit in memory forever.

In an interview: "I'd put a cache-aside layer in front of the book service, LRU eviction with a TTL of a few minutes. LRU keeps the hot catalog in memory; the TTL bounds how stale a book can get if an invalidation is missed."
